IN THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL FOR ELECTRICITY
(Appellate Jurisdiction)

Hon’ble Mr. Virender Bhat, Judicial Member
In the matter of:
Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited
Through the Superintending Engineer

Maharashtra – 441614

Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 1 of 10

Counsel for the Appellant(s) : Buddy A. Ranganadhan, Sr. Adv.
Shashwat Kumar
Rahul Chouhan
Harshit Goyal
Mukut Choudhary for App. 1
Counsel for the Respondent(s) : for Res. 1
J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The Appellant, Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution
Company Ltd. (in short “MSEDCL”) is aggrieved by the order dated
01.08.2024 of the 1st Respondent - Maharashtra Electricity
Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the
Commission”) in case No. 174/2023 filed by the 2nd Respondent
seeking implementation of earlier order dated 05.12.2020 passed by
the Commission in its favour in case No. 166 of 2020.
2. While partly allowing the case No. 174 of 2023, the
Commission has passed certain adverse observations against the
Appellant in paragraph No. 9.5 of the impugned order and has also
imposed penalty of Rs. One lac on the S.E., Gondia of the Appellant
to be recovered from his pocket. For the sake of clarity, we extract
the said paragraph No. 9.5 of the impugned order hereunder :
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 2 of 10

“9.5. Having ruled as above, the Commission cannot
ignore MSEDCL’s casual approach towards proceedings
before this Commission. The present Petition has been
registered on E-filing Portal on 21 August 2023 and vide
notice dated 22 August 2023, MSEDCL was directed to file
its reply within 15 days. Subsequently notice for E-Hearing
was issued on 6 May 2024. But MSEDCL failed to file any
submission till the date of E-Hearing i.e. 21 May 2024.
During the hearing, the Commission has specifically
directed MSEDCL to file its reply on TFAPL’s computation.
But again, MSEDCL has failed to file any submission. The
Commission in its earlier Orders have recorded strong
displeasure about non-fling of replies by MSEDCL on
timely manner. But still, such incidences are repeating.
Hence, the Commission is forced to impose penalty of Rs
1,00,000/- (Rs. One Lacs Only) on the Superintending
Engineer, Gondia, MSEDCL. Said penalty amount be paid
from pocket from concerned Officer and be deposited in
MERC Office within 15 days from date of this Order.”
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 3 of 10

3. These adverse observations as well as the imposition of
penalty upon an officer of the Appellant have been assailed in this
appeal.
4. We have heard Mr. Buddy A. Ranganadhan, Learned Senior
Counsel for the Appellant. We may note that the Appeal is not
contested by either of the two respondents as neither have they filed
any response to the appeal nor did any counsel appear on their behalf
to advance arguments.
5. Accordingly, we have perused the impugned order as well as
the grounds of appeal and have considered arguments advanced by
the Learned Senior Counsel for the Appellant.
6. In our considered opinion, the impugned order of the
Commission suffers from fundamental errors and cannot be
sustained for various reasons.
7. It was pointed out during the course of hearing by the Learned
Senior Counsel for the Appellant that Appellant had actually filed reply
to the petition of the 2nd Respondent vide e-mail on 15.05.2024 even
though belatedly, but the Commission has not taken note of it and
has incorrectly recorded in the impugned paragraph No. 9.5 of the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 4 of 10

order that no reply has been filed by the Appellant. He further pointed
out that in pursuance to order dated 21.03.2024, the Appellant had
submitted its calculations vide email dated 10.07.2024 but again the
Commission ignored the same and proceeded to record incorrectly
that the Appellant has not filed any response to the computation of
2nd Respondent.
8. We note that Appellant had filed a review petition also before
the Commission against the impugned order dated 01.08.2024 which
was dismissed vide order dated 22.01.2025. In the said review order,
the Commission has acknowledged that Appellant had filed reply to
the petition vide email dated 15.05.2024 and had submitted
calculations vide email dated 10.07.2024. The relevant extract of the
said order is as under :-
“2. Petitioner said at Para 2 that he has filed the reply
through Email which was required to be filed in E filing
portal of MERC. Even this reply which was to be filed within
15 days from the notice issued by Hon’ble Commission
which was issued on dt. 22/8/2023 with clear direction to
file the reply on E filing portal within 15 days but as per the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 5 of 10

petitioner he has filed the reply through Email. This mail
was submitted to Commission on dt. 15/5/2024 i.e. after
about 9 months from the date of notice violating the
Commissions directions.
3. On dt. 21/5/2024 during E hearing Hon’ble
Commission directed TFAPL & MSEDCL to submit the
interest calculation sheet within 7 days. TFAPL submitted
the calculation on dt. 23/5/2024 i.e. within 2 days but the
present Petitioner submitted the reply on 10/7/2024 i.e.
after about 50 days from the date of E hearing that too on
Email without filing on E filing portal again violating the
Commissions directions.”
9. Considering these admitted factual aspects, we wonder as how
did the Commission state in paragraph 9.5 of the impugned order that
Appellant has failed to file reply as directed vide notice dated
22.08.2023 and reply to the computation of 2nd Respondent as
directed during the hearing dated 21.05.2024. Both these replies had
been received in the Commission’s office vide email albeit not within
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 6 of 10

the time stipulated by the Commission. Therefore, the observations
of Commission in this regard in paragraph No. 9.5 are ex-facie
incorrect thereby dislodging completely the basis on which penalty of
Rs.1 lac was imposed.
10. The Commission ought to have recorded the delayed filing of
replies by the Appellant in the impugned order and then proceeded
to either discard those as having been filed beyond the stipulated time
or upon condoning the delay (with or without costs) considered the
replies while writing the final order. A judicial or a quasi judicial forum
cannot simply ignore any pleadings or document on record. A
reference to all the material pleadings or documents on record must
be made in the final order followed by the reasons for discarding the
same.
11. Hence, the procedure followed by the Commission in the
impugned order by ignoring the replies filed by the Appellant without
giving any reasons therefore, is vitiated and invalid in the eyes of law
which makes the entire order legally untenable and unsustainable.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 7 of 10

12. As a sequitur, imposing penalty upon the officer of the Appellant
in pursuance to such procedural irregularity also cannot be sustained
and deserves to be set aside.
13. Further, on the aspect of the imposition of penalty also, we find
that the impugned order smacks of arbitrariness and lack of cogent
reasoning. We concur with the submissions of the Learned Senior
Counsel for the Appellant that imposition of penalty upon a specific
officer of an organization is a serious matter and cannot be ordered
in a routine or cavalier manner without first putting the concerned
officer to notice about the perceived defaults attributed to him. A
punitive order like the one with which we are dealing ought not to have
been passed without following the principles of natural justice. The
office of the Appellant upon whom the penalty has been imposed was
entitled to a show cause notice and only in case of no response from
him or upon finding his response unsatisfactory, penalty could have
been imposed. It is settled legal position that principles of natural
justice are not a mere formality but must be adhered to in letter &
spirit.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 8 of 10

14. In the instance case, the Commission has nowhere explained
in the impugned order as why it chose to impose the penalty upon
Superintending Engineer, Gondia, MSEDCL. How was he alone
responsible for the defaults of the Appellant - MSEDCL is not
discernible from the order. That apart, no show cause notice has been
issued to him before imposing such huge penalty upon him which is
in clear violation of the principles of natural justice. The penalty
appears to have been imposed in an arbitrary, illegal, unjust and
casual manner. Failure to seek explanation from the concerned
officer of Appellant before imposing penalty coupled with failure to
give proper and justified explanation for the same undermines the
legal sanctity of the impugned order.
15. Hence, in view of the above discussion, we are unable to
sustain the adverse observations against the Appellant in paragraph
No. 9.5 of the impugned order as also the imposition of penalty upon
the Superintending Engineer, Gondia on account of serious
procedure irregularity on the part of the Commission, as explained
hereinabove. In fact such procedural irregularities committed by the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 155 of 2025 Page 9 of 10

Commission go to the root of the case and render the entire impugned
order perverse and legally unsustainable.
16. Accordingly, we hereby set aside the penalty imposed upon the
Superintendent Engineer, Gondia, MSEDCL and also expunge the
adverse observations against MSEDCL contained in paragraph No.
9.5 of the impugned order. The impugned order stand modified
accordingly.
17. Appeal stands allowed in these terms. All pending IAs stand
disposed of.
Pronounced in the open court on this 3rd day of July, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The issue which had arisen for our consideration during the
hearing of these two appeals and is being addressed vide this order
is :-
“Whether these two appeals have become infructuous and
not maintainable on account of the fact that M/s Global
Energy Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 4 in Appeal No. 244 of
2016 and Respondent No. 3 in Appeal No. 245 of 2016)
has undergone Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
(CIRP) w.e.f. 2nd December, 2019 and the resolution plan
also has been approved by the National Company Law
Tribunal on 3rd July, 2024 in CP(IB) No. 2520/MB/IV/2018”.
2. It was contended on behalf of the 2nd Respondent –
Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. (MSEDCL)
that the proceedings in these two appeals pending before this
Tribunal have been shown as first entry under the contingent liability
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 3 of 15

in schedule 7 of the resolution plan and, therefore, upon approval of
the resolution plan under Section 31 of the Insolvency Bankruptcy
Code (IBC) having the effect of extinguishing the pre-existing
claims/liabilities including contingent claim/liability as well as
proceedings against GEPL, the proceedings of the instant two
appeals cannot be continued and the same ought to be disposed off
as having become infructuous.
3. Learned Counsel for MSEDCL would submit that the IBC
provides “Clean Slate Principle” whereby the successful resolution
applicant takes over the corporate debtor free from past
encumbrances in order to ensure the revival of corporate debtor
without the burden of legacy disputes as envisaged under Section
30(2), 31 and 32A of the IBC. In this background, it is contended on
behalf of the MSEDCL that the claims of the Appellants in these two
appeals for refunds/adjustments under the Final Balancing and
Settlement Mechanism (FBSM), or its challenge to deviation under
the standby power agreements executed between MSEDCL and
GEPL are pre-CIRP claims and thus cannot be agitated in law now
for the reason that these are only directed against the GEPL and
stand extinguished upon approval of resolution plan for GEPL by the
NCLT.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 4 of 15

4. These contentions on behalf of the MSEDCL have been
vehemently refuted on behalf of the Appellants and GEPL.
5. It is argued that these contentions agitated on behalf of the
MSEDCL are based on the mis-characterization of the prayers made
by the Appellants in these appeals. It is submitted that mere perusal
of the pleadings in these two appeals would make it clear that the
thrust of the appeals is against the impugned orders dated 27th April,
2015 and 28th April, 2015 passed by the 1st Respondent –
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred
to as “the Commission”) as also against the legality of the standby
power agreement executed between the MSEDCL and GEPL. In
other words, it is argued that the prayer of the Appellants is against
the Maharashtra State Load Despatch Centre (MSLDC)/MSEDCL,
the beneficiary of the impugned orders passed by the Commission as
well as standby power tariff reflected in the standby power
agreements, and not GEPL. Accordingly, it is contended that the
contentions of MSEDCL that the prayer of the Appellants in these two
appeals is directed against the GEPL is totally false statement and
runs in the teeth of the pleadings as well as prayer in their appeals.
6. We have heard Shri V.M. Kannan, Learned Counsel for the
Appellants, Shri S.K. Rungta, Learned Senior Counsel appearing for
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 5 of 15

the Respondent Commission, Mr. G. Sai Kumar, Learned Senior
Counsel appearing on behalf of Respondent No. 2 ( MSEDCL) and
Mr. Sajan Poovayya, Learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of
GEPL.
7. Before analyzing the rival submissions made on behalf of the
parties by the learned counsels, we find it apposite to briefly advert to
the facts and circumstances in which these two appeals came to be
filed by the Appellants.
8. Appeal No. 244 of 2016 is directed against the order dated 27th
April, 2015 passed by the Commission in case No. 181 of 2015
whereas Appeal No. 245 of 2016 is directed against the order dated
28th April, 2015 passed by the Commission in case No. 38 of 2015.
9. The appeals pertains to the issue of applicable commercial
terms for the settlement of deviations that arose during the course of
supply of power by GEPL to Bangalore Electricity Supply Company
Limited (BESCOM) represented by the Appellant. The underlying
power supply transaction was unique open access transaction for the
reason that despite the end consumer i.e. BESCOM being situated in
the State of Karnataka and the trader i.e. GEPL through whom the
transaction was being implemented being situated in the State of
Maharashtra. GEPL had approached MSEDCL for grant of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 6 of 15

transmission open access. MSEDCL, initially insisted that deviations
emanating during the course of power supply were to be settled as
per the Maharashtra Final Balancing and Settlement Mechanism
(FBSM) which is applicable to intrastate Maharashtra transactions.
Appellants, acting as the authorized representatives of BESCOM,
had agreed to the applicability of FBSM. However, eventually,
MSEDCL refused to grant transmission of open access on the ground
that as per order dated 17th May, 2007 passed by the Commission in
case No. 42 of 2006 which introduced the Availability Based Tariff
(ABT) Regime within Maharashtra, deviations of only State Pool
Participants (SPPs) could be settled as per the FBSM, and since
GEPL was a trader and not an SPP, it could not be accommodated
within the FBSM.
10. Aggrieved by such refusal, GEPL approached the Commission
by way of Petition No. 71 of 2014 seeking grant of transmission open
access. The petition was disposed off by the Commission vide order
dated 2nd June, 2014 observing therein that the underlying power
supply transaction was an intrastate transaction in Maharashtra and
directed MSEDCL to grant transmission open access for the same.
The Commission directed that “suitable changes should be done by
MSEDCL for commercial settlements in the existing FBSM of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 7 of 15

Maharashtra State in order to accommodate this particular STOA
transaction”.
11. Accordingly, the transaction in question was found to be an
intrastate transaction within Maharashtra and required the parties to
seek intra-state transmission open access from MSEDCL.
12. However, it is to be noted that the Commission did not grant
any blanket direction for grant of Short Term Open Access (STOA) to
GEPL for supply of Electricity to the Appellant. In fact the Commission
directed GEPL to submit the documents for requirement of STOA
upon noticing that the generator M/s Gupta Energy Private Ltd. which
has issued NOC for STOA to GEPL was in default with respect to the
payment of monthly charges. The Commission also observed that in
case GEPL wishes to continue with the same generator, M/s Gupta
Energy Pvt. Ltd. will have to clear all dues.
13. In pursuance to the said order dated 2nd June, 2014 of the
Commission, Maharashtra State Load Despatch Centre (MSLDC)
issued letter dated 9th June, 2014 requiring GEPL and the Appellant
to comply with the certain conditions and submit necessary
documents including a standby agreement with MSEDCL.
Subsequent thereto, a standby agreement dated 13th June, 2015 was
reached between GEPL and MSEDCL for supply of electricity to the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 8 of 15

Appellant. In terms of the said agreement, MSEDCL was made
entitled to charge either the temporary tariff or UI charges whichever
is higher in the event of over-drawl by the Appellant. Further clause
1 of the agreement made it obligatory upon GEPL to ensure that the
complete requirement of open access in normal course shall be met
through its own generator without depending upon MSEDCL.
14. Thus GEPL and the Appellant agreed for levy of either
temporary tariff or UI charges whichever is higher in the event of over-
drawl for supply of electricity to the Appellant. Accordingly, power
supply to the Appellant w.e.f. 11th July, 2014 was in terms of the said
standby power agreement. GEPL had even made part payments in
this regard to MSEDCL.
15. The Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) executed between
GEPL and BESCOM was also duly amended in order to textually and
fully incorporate the FBSM.
16. It appears that subsequently, GEPL felt aggrieved by the fact
that inspite of order dated 2nd June, 2014 of the Commission
mandating the transaction to be accommodated within FBSM,
MSEDCL commenced charging non FBSM and high penal tariffs for
over-drawl by BESCOM and also treated the underdrawn units as
lapsed. GEPL filed case bearing No. 181 of 2014 before the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 9 of 15

Commission praying for direction for settlement of deviations in terms
of the FBSM. A similar prayer appears to have been made by GEPL
in another case No. 38 of 2015 filed before the Commission.
17. Both these petitions were dismissed by the Commission vide
orders dated 27th April, 2015 and 28th April, 2015 respectively thereby
upholding the charging of temporary tariffs for supply of electricity to
the Appellant in terms of the said standby power agreement and
holding that the arrangements between the parties as incorporated in
the standby power agreement is within the FBSM mechanism in the
peculiar facts of the case.
18. GEPL assailed both these orders by way of separate appeals
before this Tribunal. Order dated 27th April, 2015 passed in case No.
181 of 2014 was challenged in Appeal No. 111 of 2015 and order
dated 28th April, 2015 passed in case No. 38 of 2015 was impugned
in appeal No. 112 of 2015.
19. During the pendency of these appeals before this Tribunal,
GEPL entered into a fresh standby agreement dated 29th August,
2015 which contained terms and conditions for supply of electricity to
the Appellant w.e.f. 1st July, 2015. At the same time, the Appellant
entered into a supplemental PPA dated 1st October, 2015 with
GEPL. At this juncture, the Appellant herein sought to intervene in
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 10 of 15

these two appeals and filed applications bearing IA No. 399 of 2015
(in Appeal No. 111 of 2015) and IA No. 400 of 205 (in Appeal No. 112
of 2015) in this regard.
20. However, it appears that there had been some agreement
between GEPL and MSEDCL requiring GEPL to withdraw these two
appeals and accordingly based upon such agreements between the
parties, both the appeals came to be dismissed as withdrawn by this
Tribunal vide order dated 28th October, 2015. As a sequitur, the IA
No. 399 of 2015 and IA No. 400 of 2015 filed by the Appellant were
disposed off having become infructuous. The relevant portion of the
said order dated 28th October, 2015 of this Tribunal is extracted
herein below:-
“Since as per the agreement of the parties, both these
appeals are to be withdrawn unconditionally and there is
no dispute between the rival parties regarding execution
of this document. This document is accordingly, accepted
and both the appeals being Nos. 111 of 2015 and 112 of
2015 are hereby ordered to be withdrawn. However, there
is no order as to costs.
So far as I.A. No.400 of 2015 in Appeal No.111 of 2015
and I.A. No.399 of 2015 in Appeal No.112 of 2015 seeking
impleadment on behalf of power company of Karnataka
Ltd. and Bangalore Electricity Supply company Ltd. as
respondents in these appeals is concerned, the same are
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 11 of 15

already on record of these appeals. Since the main
appeals have been ordered to be withdrawn and there
remains to substance now in allowing the aforesaid
impleadment applications.
In view of above, the aforementioned interim applications
(IAs) are hereby disposed of as being infructuous.”
21. The Appellant approached Hon’ble Supreme Court challenging
the said dismissal of its applications by the Tribunal vide said order
dated 28th October, 2015. The Civil Appeal Nos. 911 & 912 of 2016
filed in this regard by the Appellant were disposed off by the Apex
court vide order dated 15th February, 2016, relevant part of which is
reproduced herein below”-
“Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, the learned Attorney General for
India, appearing on behalf of the appellant, has submitted
that the appellant would like to withdraw these appeals so
as to file appeals before the Appellate Tribunal for
Electricity, Principal Bench, New Delhi. Permission is
granted with liberty to approach the Tribunal.
The civil appeals are disposed of as withdrawn.”
22. It is in these circumstances that the Appellant has approached
this Tribunal by way of the instant two appeals. The Appeal No. 244
of 2016 is directed against the order dated 28th April, 2015 passed by
the Commission which had earlier been impugned in Appeal No. 112
of 2015 whereas Appeal No. 245 of 2016 is directed against the order
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 12 of 15

dated 27th April, 2015 passed by the Commission which had earlier
been impugned by way of Appeal No. 111 of 2015.
23. It cannot be gainsaid that both the Impugned orders dated 27th
April, 2015 and 28th April, 2015 of the Commission are in favour of
MSEDCL and against the GEPL. These orders uphold the levy of
standby power purchase/temporary tariff by MSEDCL in contrast to
FBSM rates due to which MSEDCL as well as MSLDC have become
richer. The prayer of the Appellant in the two appeals is to direct that
the commercial settlement of overdrawl/underdrawl/standby power
qua transactions between the Appellant and MSLDC has to be
commercially settled based upon FBSM mechanism vide order dated
2nd June, 2014 passed in case No. 71 of 2014.
24. We feel in agreement with the submission of the Learned
Counsel for the Appellant that the thrust of the appeal is against the
legality as well as validity of the orders dated 27th April, 2015 and 28th
April, 2015 passed by the Commission as well as that of standby
power agreement executed between the GEPL and MSEDCL. It is,
therefore, evident that the appeals assail the action of
MSEDCL/MSLDC whereby MSEDCL has been levying temporary
tariff for the power supply by GEPL to Appellant instead of resorting
to FBSM mechanism. Thus, the prayer of the Appellant in the two
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 13 of 15

appeals is not directly against the GEPL and is manifestly against the
MSEDCL which has been the beneficiary under the two impugned
orders passed by the Commission.
25. It is also evident that in case the Appellant succeeds in these
two appeals, MSEDCL would be required to reimburse excess money
levied by it from GEPL, to GEPL.
26. Perusal of relevant clauses of the resolution plan approved by
NCLT, Mumbai would reveal that any claim of 3rd party against GEPL
does not survive as on date of the approval of the said plan but on
the other hand, the claims initiated by GEPL against any 3rd party
would continue to exist.
27. “Clean Slate” Principle or Doctrine as elucidated in various
judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court envisages that the claims
against the corporate debtor stand extinguished upon approval of the
resolution plan under Section 31 of IBC. However, it does not apply
to the proceedings which, if successful, would enhance and protect
the assets or rights of the corporate debtor or which are against the
3rd party and not against the corporate debtor.
28. The adjudication of these two appeals and any final order
passed thereupon would not result in crystallization of any liability
upon GEPL. On the contrary, if the appeals are allowed and the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 244 & 245 of 2016 Page 14 of 15

impugned orders are set aside, the GEPL would stand to benefit as it
would be entitled to receive some money from MSEDCL.
29. In the light of the above discussion, we hold that there is no
merit in the contentions agitated on behalf of MSEDCL that the instant
appeals have become infructuous as well as non-maintainable upon
approval of resolution plan qua GEPL by the NCLT, Mumbai.
30. It is manifest that the approval of resolution plan for GEPL by
NCLT, Mumbai on 3rd July, 2014 will not have any impact upon these
two appeals as well as their outcome for the reason that any final
order to be passed in these two appeals would not fasten any liability
upon GEPL and to the contrary, GEPL would stand to benefit from
such order as it may be entitled to receive some money from
MSEDCL.
31. Therefore, let the proceedings of these two appeals continue.
The appeals shall be heard on merits.
32. List the appeals for hearing before the Regular Bench of Court-
II on 13.08.2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

1. The Appellant, M/s Radiance Punjab Renewable Private
Limited is assailing the order dated 4th June, 2018 passed by 1st
Respondent Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission
(hereinafter referred to as "the Commission") passed in Petition No. 24
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 2 of 52

of 2016 which was filed by M/s. Azure Renewable Energy Pvt. Ltd.,
(the predecessor in interest of the Appellant herein) seeking extension
of the commercial operation date of its solar power generation sites
beyond the schedule commercial operation date with further prayer for
entitlement to tariff of Rs.7.59 per kWh in terms of the PPA dated 31st
March, 2015 executed between the Appellant and the 2nd Respondent
Punjab State Power Corporation Limited. Various Force Majeure
events were agitated by the Appellant in the petition which, according
to it, prevented it from achieving commercial operation on or before the
scheduled date. Vide the impugned order, the Commission has
condoned delay of only 29 days and has disallowed the claims of the
Appellant with regards to the majority of the Force Majeure events and
thus tariff for the solar power project sites of the Appellant was reduced
from Rs.7.59 per unit to Rs.5.09 per unit.
Description of the Parties :-
2. The Appellant is a generating company within the meaning of
Section 2(28) of the Electricity Act, 2003 and is a solar power
developer. The 2nd Respondent - Punjab State Power Corporation
Limited is an unbundled entity of the erstwhile Punjab State Electricity
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 3 of 52

Board and is vested with the distribution of electricity in the State of
Punjab.
3. The 3rd Respondent - Punjab Energy Development Authority
is a designated agency in the State of Punjab for development of
power projects and was the designated agency to conduct the
competitive bidding process on behalf of the 2nd Respondent - PSPCL
for procurement of electricity from solar generation projects.
Facts of the case
4. The facts and circumstances of the case in which the above
said appeal has arisen are noted hereunder.
5. Vide notification dated 26th December, 2012, the Government
of Punjab notified the New and Renewable Source of Energy Policy,
2012 (in short NRSE 2012) providing for various incentives and
benefits to renewable energy projects to be established in the State of
Punjab. The policy provided for the terms and conditions on the basis
of which the projects were to be established, the benefits to be granted
to the projects and also the tariff at which power was to be procured
by the Distribution Licensees i.e. the 2nd Respondent from such
projects. It also envisaged that the 3rd Respondent - PEDA to be a
nodal agency as a project facilitator for all such projects. PEDA was
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 4 of 52

given the responsibility of "Single Window Clearance" for all sanctions
and clearances from the Government departments within a period of
60 days in order to ensure seamless commissioning of renewable
energy power plants.
6. The bids/proposals for establishment of Solar RoofTop Projects
under Section 63 of Electricity Act, 2003 were invited against RFP by
PEDA in January, 2015 through e-bidding system.
7. The Appellant participated in the bidding in March, 2015 and
was declared successful bidder on 25th March, 2015 for capacity of 10
MW solar rooftop power project under category II bidders to establish
a power plant and supply power to 2nd Respondent - PSPCL for a
period of 25 years at net tariff of Rs.7.59 per kWh in accordance with
the provisions of RFP. The Appellant was required to submit
performance security by way of irrevocable Bank Guarantee at the rate
of Rs.40 lakhs per MW aggregating to Rs.4 crores and to sign the
Implementation Agreement (IA) with PEDA within 5 days of the date of
the issue of Letter of Award (LoA) and subsequently to sign Power
Purchase Agreement (PPA) with 2nd Respondent - PSPCL.
8. The Appellant executed Implementation Agreement with PEDA
on 28th March, 2015 and also submitted the required performance
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 5 of 52

guarantee in the amount of Rs.4 crores to PEDA in terms of Article
6.2(iv) of the IA. As per the terms of RfP & IA, the Solar Rooftop
Projects were to be commissioned by the Appellant within 10 months
from the date of signing of PPA.
9. The solar power developers including the Appellant were
invited by the 2nd Respondent - PSPCL on 31st March, 2015 to sign
the PPAs. The PPAs contained a clause No. 35 providing that the PPA
shall be effective and binding only upon approval by the Commission
and would be subject to the conditions, if any, to be stipulated by the
Commission.
10. The 2nd Respondent PSPCL filed Petition No. 23 of 2015
before the Commission seeking approval to procure electricity from the
solar power developers as well as to approve the PPAs executed by it
with them. The petition was allowed by the Commission on 11th May,
2015 and accordingly the PPAs were approved.
11. Thereafter, the Appellant identified the roofs for the entire 10
MW project and submitted the details to PEDA vide letter dated 26th
August, 2015.
12. It appears that PEDA issued a notice dated 3rd September,
2015 to the Appellant for termination of the LOA on the ground of not
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 6 of 52

providing the list of properties for installing solar power projects as per
clause 4.1 (vii) of the Implementation Agreement. The Appellant sent
a detailed response dated 29th September, 2015 to the said notice of
PEDA mentioning therein the difficulties in identifying the rooftops of
which the solar power projects were to be installed.
13. Meanwhile the Appellant, also vide letter dated 4th September,
2015, sought feasibility clearance for the entire power project from the
planning department of PSPCL. Vide letter dated 7th September, 2015,
the Appellant sought feasibility/technical clearance from PEDA for
implementation of the project at nine individual sites.
14. PEDA gave concurrence for setting up of SPV plants identified
by the Appellant on 14th October, 2015 copy of which was also marked
to PSPCL. The Appellant immediately addressed a letter dated 15th
October, 2015 to PSPCL with the request for immediate
feasibility/connectivity/ technical approval for evacuation of power from
the 10 MW distributed capacity of the rooftop SPV plant at 11KV GSS
at various locations.
15. In subsequent letter dated 26th August, 2015, PEDA wrote to
PSPCL that at the time of signing of Implementation Agreement, the
Company i.e. the Appellant had informed that it has not identified any
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 7 of 52

location for setting up of the project and now the Appellant has
identified the rooftop areas and therefore supplementary PPA for 10
MW rooftop SPV plant has to be signed. Accordingly, the Appellant
wrote a letter dated 28th October, 2015 to PSPCL requesting it to
execute supplementary PPA with regards to the identified rooftop sites.
Instead of executing the supplementary PPA, PSPCL wrote a letter
dated 4th November, 2015 to PEDA with the request to first carry out
amendment in the Implementation Agreement before supplementary
PPA can be executed.
16. On 10th November, 2015, PEDA executed amended
Implementation Agreement with the Appellant specifying therein the
nine sites identified by the Appellant. This fact was intimated to PSPCL
by PEDA vide letter dated 13th November, 2015 with the request to
carry out amendments in the PPA with the Appellant.
17. On 13th November, 2015, the Appellant also requested PSPCL
to carry out requisite amendment in the PPA so that the Appellant
could set up its SPV plant in timely manner. Vide letter dated 18th
November, 2015 PSPCL again sought clarification regarding
installation of projects at several sites. This position was clarified by
PEDA vide letter dated 20th November, 2015 stating that setting up of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 8 of 52

the project at different sites was permissible as per the RFP document
and again requested PSPCL to carry out the requisite amendment in
the PPA.
18. However, PSPCL again, vide letter dated 24th November, 2015,
requested PEDA to relook into the matter. Thereafter, vide letter dated
26th November, 2015 PEDA again requested PSPCL to sign the
amended PPA with the Appellant clarifying that it was extremely
difficult to get a large single rooftop area of one lakh sq. meter in the
State of Punjab.
19. Ultimately, the PSPCL carried out necessary amendments in
the PPA on 2nd December, 2015 specifying therein the names of
identified cites for setting up of the solar power plant by the Appellant.
Subsequently, on 7th December, 2015, PSPCL gave technical
concurrence for these sites of the Appellant.
20. On 17th December, 2015, the Appellant addressed the letter to
PSPCL with the request to expedite the grant of grid connectivity which
was required to start the process of execution of the project in the
timely manner. This was followed by reminder dated 28th December,
2015. PSPCL gave grid feasibility to two rooftop sites of the Appellant
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 9 of 52

on the same day i.e. 28th December, 2015 and for seven remaining
sites on 31st December, 2015.
21. The Appellant along with other solar power developers sent a
representation dated 6th January, 2016 to PEDA mentioning therein
the circumstances in which approval of PPA was delayed much, in
turn, resulting in delay achieving financial closure as well as
disbursement of loan. However, PEDA vide letter dated 18th January,
2016 informed them that there will be no extension in the Schedule
Commissioning Date (SCOD) of the power projects.
22. The Appellant received a communication dated 24th February,
2016 from PEDA asking it to intimate the extent of capacity which has
been commissioned by the Appellant in the month of February, 2016.
PEDA also sought to impose penalty for non-commissioning /short fall
in the commissioning of allocated capacity as per clause 3.23 of RFP.
The Appellant submitted a detailed response dated 26th February,
2016 to the said letter of PEDA.
23. Thereafter, during 1st February, 2016 to 2nd May, 2016, PSPCL
approved the route of transmission lines.
24. In these circumstances, the Appellant approached the
Commission with Petition No. 24 of 2016 seeking extension of SCOD
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 10 of 52

of the solar power project till 31st May, 2016 with applicable tariff of
Rs.7.59 per kWh and further direction to PSPCL as well as PEDA not
to take any coercive action against the Appellant with regard to the
Performance Bank Guarantee deposited by the Appellant. The prayers
made in the petition by the Appellant are extracted herein below:-
(a) set aside and / or quash the letters dated 18.01.2016 and
24.02.2016 of PEDA;
(b) hold and declare that the Commercial Operation Date of
the project of the petitioner stands extended till 31.05.2016 in
accordance with clause 10 of the PPA read with Article 7.0 of
the IA on account of force majeure events which are beyond
the control of the petitioner;
and
further hold and declare that the Commercial Operation Date
of the two sites / plants of the petitioner i.e. PSAMB Ludhiana
and Canam Consultants stands extended till 8th June, 2016
and 22nd June, 2016 respectively, in accordance with Article
10 of the PPA read with Article 7.0 of the Implementation
Agreement on account of Force Majeure events and events
which are beyond the control of the petitioner.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 11 of 52

(c) hold and declare that the petitioner is entitled to tariff of Rs.
7.59 per kWh (levellised tariff) in terms of the PPA dated
31.03.2015 during the extended COD period;
(d) direct PEDA not to invoke the Performance Bank
Guarantee, and to not take any coercive actions whatsoever
against the petitioner.
25. The petition has been decided by the Commission vide order
dated 4th June, 2018 which is impugned in this appeal. Vide the said
impugned order, the Commission has condoned the delay of 29 days
which had occasioned due to delay on the part of the PSPCL in
granting grid feasibility clearance but has rejected the remaining Force
Majeure claims of the appellant thereby causing reduction of tariff for
the Appellant's solar power project from Rs.7.59 per unit to Rs.5.09
per unit.
26. It is the contention of the Appellant in this appeal that delays on
account of following events ought to have been taken into account by
the Commission in the impugned order and accordingly, the SCOD of
the power project ought to have been extended;
(a) Delay of 41 days in approval of PPA.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 12 of 52

(b) Delay in grid connectivity and in execution of (b) supplementary
PPA.
(c) Delay on account of JAT agitation.
27. We have heard Learned Counsel for the Appellant as well as
Learned Counsel for Respondent Nos. 1, 2 & 3. We have also perused
the written submissions filed by the Learned Counsels.
Relevant contractual clauses :-
28. Before embarking upon to discuss these issues raised in the
Appeal by the Appellant, we find it pertinent to refer to various
provisions of the RFP document, Implementation Agreement and the
PPA/SPPA.
29. Clause 3.2(B) of the RFP document relates to the scope of work
and provides that the scope of work for the bidder include identification
of buildings/leasing rooftop of buildings, obtaining No Objection
Certificate from PSPCL for grid connectivity, complete design,
engineering, manufacture, supply, storage, civil work, erection, testing
& commissioning of the grid connected rooftop solar PV project
including operation of maintenance of the project. Therefore, it was the
responsibility of the bidder to identify the rooftops upon which the
allocated solar power project was intended to be installed.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 13 of 52

30. Clause 3.9 of the RFP is with regards to the Implementation
Agreement and is extracted hereinbelow :-
"Implementation Agreement (IA)
The terms and condition for Implementation of the project shall
be formulized through signing of Implementation Agreement
between successful bidder and PEDA. The Solar Project
Developer shall be required to pay non refundable facilitation
service charges @ 0.5% of the total Project Cost (as per the
project cost given in the Detailed Project Report (DPR) submitted
by the SPD) with a maximum limit of Rs. 50,00,000/- (Rupees Fifty
Lac only) before signing of Implementation Agreement.
The successful bidder shall execute separate Implementation
Agreement for each individual projects and shall pay separate
facilitation charges.
The detailed project report shall be submitted by the SPD
before signing of IA. The IA is attached as Annexure-4.”
31. Clause 3.10 of the RFP provided that the PPA shall be
executed between PSPCL and selected bidder within 30 days from the
date of signing of the Implementation Agreement and would be valid
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 14 of 52

for 25 years from the date of commissioning of the complete plant or
partial capacity. As per clause 3.23 of the RFP, the Rooftop Solar PV
project was to be commissioned within 10 months from the date of
signing of the PPA and in case of failure to do so, PEDA was entitled
to encash Performance Bank Guarantee in the following manner :-
(a) Delay upto one month PEDA will encash 30% of the total
Performance Bank Guarantee proportionate to the Capacity
not commissioned.
(b) Delay of more than one month and upto two month, PEDA
will encash remaining 70% of the total Performance Bank
Guarantee proportionate to the Capacity not commissioned.
(c) The penalty on the delay in project commissioning as
stated above will be calculated on the number of days for
which delay occurs on pro-rate basis.
(d) in case of part commissioning, the penalty shall be
calculated on the delay on un-commissioned capacity. In case
the commissioning of project is delayed beyond 12 months
from the date of signing of PPA, the Project Developer shall
pay to PSPCL the Liquidated Damages at a rate of Rs.
20,000/- (Rupees Twenty Thousand Rupees Only) per MW
per day for delay in such remaining Capacity which is not
commissioned. The maximum time period allowed for
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 15 of 52

commissioning of the full Project Capacity with encashment of
Performance Bank Guarantees and payment of Liquidated
Damages shall be limited to 15 months from the date of signing
of PPA. The amount of liquidated damages worked out as
above shall be recovered by PSPCL from the payments due
to the Project Developer on account of sale of solar power to
PSPCL. In case, the Commissioning of the Project is delayed
beyond 15 months from the date of signing of PPA, the PPA
capacity shall stand reduced/amended to the Project Capacity
Commissioned and the PPA for the balance Capacity will
stand terminated and shall be reduced from the selected
Project Capacity. The LOA & IA shall also stand terminated for
the balance un-commissioned capacity.
Note :-If due to delay COD of the project shifts beyond 31st
March 2016 then in accordance to CERC Regulations the
tariff shall cease to exist and the project developer should
be required to get the tariff afresh by filing the petition in
PSERC.
Part Commissioning:
Part commissioning of the Project shall be accepted by PEDA
subject to the condition that the minimum capacity for
acceptance of part commissioning shall be 0.501 MW.
The PPA will remain in force for a period of 25 years from the
date of acceptance of part commissioning of the Project."
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 16 of 52

32. Article 3 of the Implementation Agreement dated 28th March,
2015 executed between the Appellant and PEDA provides that in case
the COD of the project crosses beyond 31st March, 2016 the tariff
mentioned in the agreement shall cease to exist and the developer will
be bound to get tariff re-determined from the Commission.
33. Article 6 of the IA also is material and is extracted hereinbelow:-
"6.1 Obligations of PEDA:
PEDA will provide necessary support including Single
Window Clearances to facilitate the development of the
projects. This may include facilitation in assisting and
advising in respect of obtaining various approvals from
the Government Departments. However, it will be the
sole responsibility of the Company to obtain such
Approvals.
6.2 Obligations of Company:
i The Company shall act as per the terms and
conditions of RfP;
ii. In case of Consortium, the share holding pattern
and Controlling Shareholding pattern (held by the Lead
Member holding more than 50% of the voting rights) shall
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 17 of 52

not change from the date of submission of RfP up to one
year after the commissioning of the Project.
iii. Power Purchase Agreement (PPA):
The PPA shall be executed between PSPCL and the
Selected Bidder(s), on or before 31st March 2015 after
signing of Implementation Agreement. However, PPA will
remain in force for 25 (Twenty five) years from the date
of Commercial Operation.
iv. Performance Bank Guarantee:
The Company has submitted Performance Bank
Guarantees(s) of Rs. 40,00,000/- (Rupees Forty Lac
Only) per MW for each project at the time of signing of IA
as per the Format - 6.3 B of RfP and other terms and
conditions mentioned in Section 3 of RfP thereof. The
Performance Bank Guarantee shall be valid for a period
of 15 months from the date of signing of IA.
v. Technology:
The Company shall submit a certificate from the project /
its client, situated anywhere in world that the technology
proposed to be supplied by the Manufacturer /
Technology Provider is in successful operation for at least
one year.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 18 of 52

The Company shall promote only commercially
established and operational technologies to minimize the
technology risk and to achieve the timely commissioning
of the Projects.
vi. Rooftop for Construction of Solar PV Power
Project :
The Bidder / SPD shall acquire rooftop on ownership
/leasehold basis for 30 years. The rooftop area
approximately 100000 Sq. foot per MW shall be in clear
possession of the project developer. In this regard the
Project Developer shall be required to furnish the
documentary evidences i.e. Regd. Sale deed of building
showing ownership/regd. Rooftop lease deed of building
in the name of SPD to PEDA within 120 days from issue
of Letter of Award.
vii. Commissioning of Project:
The Rooftop Solar PV Project shall be commissioned
within 10 (Ten) months from the date of signing of PPA.
viii. Grid Feasibility Letter from PSPCL:
The Company shall obtain and submit to PEDA the grid
feasibility letter from PSPCL within 120 days from the
date of signing of PPA."
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 19 of 52

34. Article 10 of the Implementation Agreement defines Force
Majeure and provides consequences thereof. The same is extracted
hereinbelow:-
“ARTICLE 10: FORCE MAJEURE
10.1 Force Majeure Event
In this Agreement, Force Majeure means an event occurrence in
India of any or all of non-political events described in clause 10.2
and political events described in clause 10.3 respectively hereinafter
which prevents the party claiming Force Majeure. (The affected
party) from performing its obligations under this agreement and
which act or event,
i. Is beyond the reasonable control of and not arising out of the
fault of the affected party.
ii. The affected party has been unable to prevent by the exercise
of due diligence and reasonable efforts, skill and care,
including through expenditure of reasonable sum of money
and
iii. Has a materially adverse effect on the project.
10.2 Non-political force majeure events
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 20 of 52

For the purpose of 10.1 non-political force majeure events shall
mean one or more of the following acts or events:
i) Acts of God or events beyond the reasonable control of the
affected party which could not reasonably have been expected
to occur such as extreme adverse weather or environment
conditions, lighting, heavy rains, cyclones, tempest, whirlwind,
landslides, storms, floods, volcanic, eruptions or fire (to the
extent originating from the source external to the site or not
designed for in construction works);
ii) Radioactive contamination or ionising radiation;
iii) An act of war (whether declared of undeclared) invasion,
armed conflict or act of foreign enemy, unexpected call up of
armed forces, embargo, blockade, rebellion, riot religious
strike, bombs or civil commotion, sabotage terrorism;
iv) Strikes or boycotts interrupting operations of the project
continuing for at least 7 days;
v) Any judgement or order of any court of competent jurisdiction
or statutory authority in India made against the Company in
any proceedings for the reason other than failure of the
Company to comply with any applicable law or clearance or
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 21 of 52

on account of breach thereof, with any applicable law or
clearance or on account of breach thereof, or of any contract,
or enforcement of this Agreement or exercise of any of its
rights under this Agreement by PEDA; or
vi) Any other event or circumstances of nature analogues to the
foregoing.
10.3 Political Force Majeure Event
Political Events shall mean one or more of the following acts or
events by or an account of PEDA, GoP, Gol or any other
Government Agency or Statutory Authority.
i) Change in law.
ii) Expropriation or compulsory confiscation, by any Government
Agency of any Project Assets-or rights of the Company.
iii) The unlawful or un-authorised or without jurisdiction
revocation of, or refusal to renew or grant without valid clause
any consent or approval required by the Company to perform
its obligations under the Agreement (Other than a consent the
obtaining of which is a condition precedent) provided that such
delay, modification, denial, refusal or revocation did not result
from the Company's inability or failure to comply with any
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 22 of 52

condition relating to grant, maintenance or renewal of such
consent or permits.
10.4 Notification obligations
If a party is affected by any force Majeure event, the affected party
shall give the other parties written notice describing the particulars
of the Force Majeure event as soon as reasonably practicable after
its occurrence but not later than five days after the date on which
such party knew of the commencement of the Force Majeure event
or of its effect on such party.”
35. Coming to the Power Purchase Agreement dated 31st March,
2015 executed between the Appellant and PSPCL. It is stated in its
preamble that the Implementation Agreement signed between the
Appellant and PEDA shall be treated as an integral part of the PPA
and all the clauses as well as regulatory norms applicable to the
Implementation Agreement shall be unequivocally applicable to the
Power Purchase Agreement in letter and spirit. Article 10 of the PPA
relates to the commissioning of the power project and is extracted
hereinbelow :-
“10.0.0 FACILITY COMMISSIONING OF GENERATING FACILITY
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 23 of 52

10.1.0 The Generating Company shall commission the
Generating Facility (which shall be Scheduled Date of Commercial
Operation) and synchronize with the PSPCL/PSTCL's Grid within 10
months from the Effective Date i.e. date of signing of this PPA which
is 31st March 2015. Therefore, the scheduled date of commissioning
for this project is 31st January, 2016.
In case of delay after the scheduled date of commissioning within
grace period of further two months i.e. 12 months from the date of
signing of PPA, with forfeiture of performance B.G. by PEDA, the
commissioning date for the project shall be 31 March, 2016.
In case of further delay in commissioning beyond 12 months but
within 15 months from the date of signing of PPA, with applicable
liquidated damages payable to PSPCL as per Clause 10.1.1, the
revised commissioning date of the project shall be 31st June, 2016.
10.1.1 In case there is delay in commissioning of project
beyond 12 months from the effective date then the project developer
shall pay to PSPCL the liquidated damages @ 20,000/- (Rupees
Twenty Thousand Only) per MW per day for delay in such capacity
which is not commissioned. The amount of liquidated damages
worked out as above shall be recovered by PSPCL from the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 24 of 52

payments due to the Project Developer on account of sale of solar
power to PSPCL. The liquidated damage will be applicable without
prejudice to any other penalty imposed for delay in commissioning.
In case, the Commissioning of the Project is delayed beyond 15
months from the date of signing of PPA, the PPA capacity shall
stand reduced / amended to the Project Capacity Commissioned
and the PPA for the balance Capacity will stand terminated and shall
be reduced from the selected Project Capacity. The LoA & IA shall
also stand terminated for the balance un-commissioned capacity.
10.1.2 This PPA will remain valid for the capacity
commissioned within 15 months from the effective date and the
capacity for the purpose of this PPA will stand revised accordingly."
36. Article 19 of the PPA specifies the Force Majeure events and
its impact upon the rights and liabilities of the parties, the same is
extracted hereinbelow :-
19.0.0 FORCE MAJEURE
19.1.0 If any party hereto shall be wholly or partially prevented
from performing any of its obligations under this
Agreement by reason of or on account of lightning,
earthquake, fire, floods, invasion, insurrection, rebellion,
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 25 of 52

mutiny, civil unrest, riot, epidemics, explosion, the order
of any court, judge or civil authority, change in applicable
law, war, any act of God or public enemy or any other
similar cause or reason reasonably beyond its control and
not attributable to any negligent or Intentional act, error or
omission, then such party shall be excused of its
obligations/ liabilities under this Agreement and shall not
be liable for any damage, sanction or loss resulting there
from to the other party.
19.2.0 The party invoking this clause shall satisfy the other party
of the existence of any Force Majeure event and give
written notice within seven (7) days of the occurrence of
such Force Majeure event to the other party and also take
all reasonable and possible steps to eliminate, mitigate or
overcome the effect and consequence of any such Force
Majeure event.
19.3.0 In the event of a Force Majeure event or conditions, any
payment due under this Agreement shall be made as
provided herein and shall not be withheld.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 26 of 52

19.4.0 This clause as provided in this PPA will be operative after
the project achieves COD. For force majeure events
occurring during the commissioning period of the project,
provisions of IA will be applicable.”
37. Article 35 of the PPA provides that the PPA shall be effective
and binding on the parties only on approval by the Commission and
shall be subject to such condition as may be stipulated by the
Commission while granting such approvals.
38. Amended/supplementary PPAs dated 10th November, 2015
and 2nd December, 2015 specifies the names of the nine ware houses
on the rooftops of which the Appellant proposed to install the solar
power project. It is mentioned herein that all other clauses contained
in the already executed PPA dated 31st March, 2015 shall remain
unchanged.
Analysis and findings:
39. Our Analysis and findings (issue wise) is as under :-
(a) Delay of 41 days in approval of PPA.
40. It is not disputed that after the execution of the PPA between
the Appellant and the 2nd Respondent on 31st March, 2015, the 2nd
Respondent filed petition No. 23 of 2015 before the Commission
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 27 of 52

seeking approval to procure electricity from the solar power
developers as well as for approval of the PPAs executed by it with
them. The petition was allowed by the Commission on 11th May, 2015
and accordingly the PPA got approved.
41. As per Section 86(1)(b) of the Act, the State Commission is
empowered to regulate the electricity purchase and procurement
process of the Distribution Licensees including the price at which
electricity is procured from the generating companies through power
purchase agreement. Therefore, a Distribution Licensee can
procure/purchase power only in the manner and at the price as
approved by the State Commission upon satisfying the Commission
about its requirement for such power. It is for the Commission to
determine whether Distribution Licensee actually requires the power
for supply to its consumers and whether the rate quoted in the PPA
is reasonable as well as in consonance to the market conditions and
whether the Distribution Licensee can obtain such power from other
cheaper sources. Thus, it is the State Commission which regulates
the entire process of purchase and procurement of power by each
Distribution Licensee in the State by virtue of power conferred upon it
under Section 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act, 2003. In this regard, we
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 28 of 52

also find it relevant to refer Regulation 46 of Punjab State Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2005
which is quoted herein below :-
46. POWER PROCUREMENT AND PURCHASE
1. In accordance with the provisions of the Act and the licence
conditions, every Distribution Licensee shall purchase and procure
electricity required for the Licensed Business of the Distribution
Licensee in an economical and efficient manner and under a
transparent power purchase and procurement process and generally
based on the principles of purchase of electricity at the least cost.
2. The power purchase by a Distribution Licensee may be classified
by the Commission as short term power purchase and long term
power purchase on terms as may be decided by the Commission from
time to time.
3. The Commission may, from time to time, issue guidelines, practice
directions and orders governing the short term purchases and long
term purchases which the Distribution Licensee can undertake for the
purpose of the Licensed Business.
4. (a) The Distribution Licensee shall satisfy the Commission as
to the need for additional power procurement on a long term
basis
(b) The Distribution Licensee shall not enter into a binding or
enforceable contractual commitment of such long term power
purchase till the Commission by a general or special order
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 29 of 52

approves the procurement of electricity by the Distribution
Licensee.
5. Unless otherwise approved by the Commission by a general or
special order, a long term power purchase or procurement by the
Distribution Licensee shall be done through a competitive
procurement process approved by the Commission.
6. (a) The Distribution Licensee shall satisfy the Commission
that the electricity procured under long term power purchase
otherwise than through a competitive bidding process or any
short term power purchase is economical in the prevalent
circumstances and that the Distribution Licensee has made
prudent and best efforts to minimise the cost of purchase.
(b) The Commission may not permit any such long term
purchase if the manner or method proposed for such
procurement of electricity is not conducive to the objective of
least cost purchase or for any other reason the purchase is not
economical or efficient……….
(Emphasis Supplied)
42. This Regulation also makes it mandatory for Distribution
Licensee within the State of Punjab to satisfy the Commission about
its need for additional power procurement on a long-term basis and
that such procurement is economical and that Distribution Licensee
has made prudent and best efforts to minimize the cost of purchase.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 30 of 52

43. In Tata Power Company Limited vs. Reliance Energy Limited,
(2009) 16 SCC 659, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as under:-
“108. A generating company, if the liberalization and
privatization policy is to be given effect to, must be held to
be free to enter into an agreement and in particular long-
term agreement with the distribution agency; terms and
conditions of such an agreement, however, are not
unregulated. Such an agreement is subject to grant of
approval by the Commission. The Commission has a
duty to check if the allocation of power is reasonable.
If the terms and conditions relating to quantity, price,
mode of supply, the need of the distributing agency
vis-à-vis the consumer, keeping in view its long-term
need are not found to be reasonable, approval may
not be granted.
………………
115. A PPA may be a long-term one or a short-term one.
Regulations have been made by the Commission by
making the MERC (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2005. Short-term power procurement refers
to an agreement for procurement of power for a period of
less than one year. Regulation 23.1 requires the
distribution licensee to prepare a five-year plan inter alia
upon taking into consideration the sources for
procurement thereof. Regulation 24.1 mandates
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 31 of 52

obtaining of prior approval of the Commission
therefor. Approval by the Commission is granted
upon examining the process of procurement having
regard to the factors specified in Regulation 24.2. It is
in the aforementioned context that grant of approval of
PPA by and between TPC (G) on the one hand and BEST
and TPC (D), on the other hand, necessitated. The
proposal of TPC (G) that Rinfra should enter with it into a
long-term agreement assumes significance.”
(Emphasis supplied)
44. This Tribunal as in the case of Rithwik Energy Generation Pvt.
Limited vs. Karnataka Power Transmission Corp. Limited and
others, 2011 ELR (APTEL) 1651 held as under :-
“10. Let us take up the first issue regarding the validity of
the PPA. 10.1According to the learned counsel for the
appellant, the PPA is not enforceable by law as the
respondents no. 2 had already exceeded the permissible
limit of power purchase from the renewable sources of
energy as per the State Commission's Regulations and
for this reason the PPA was returned by the State
Commission on 6.6.2007. The approval of the State
Commission was mandatory under Section 25 (3) of the
Karnataka Electricity Reform Act, 1999. The PPA became
void on account of the approval not having been given by
the State Commission.
………...
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 32 of 52

10.3. Let us first examine the Section 25(3)(4) of the
Karnataka Reform Act referred to by the appellant. The
relevant extracts are reproduced below:
“25 (3) A holder of a supply or transmission licence may,
unless expressly prohibited by the terms of its licence,
enter into arrangements for the purchase of electricity
from,-
(a) The holder of a supply licence which permits the holder
of such licence to supply energy to other licensees for
distribution by them; and (b) Any person or generating
company with the consent of the Commission”.
“25(4) Any agreement relating to any transaction of the
nature described in sub-sections (1), (2), or (3) unless
made with, or subject to, such consent as aforesaid, shall
be void”.
Section 185(3) of the 2003 Act specifically stipulates that
the provisions of the enactments specified in the
schedule, which includes the Karnataka Reform Act, not
inconsistent with the provisions of the 2003 Act, shall
apply to the States in which such enactments are
applicable.”
10.4. According to Section 86 (b) of the 2003 Act, the
State Commission is empowered to requlate
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 33 of 52

electricity purchase and procurement process of the
distribution licensees including the price at which
electricity is procured from the generating companies
through agreement for purchase of power.
10.5. In view of above, the distribution licensee has to
obtain the consent of the State Commission for
procurement of power against the PPA. Unless the
State Commission gives its consent to the PPA, the
distribution licensee cannot procure power under the
PPA. Thus, the PPA will come into effect only after
obtaining the consent of the State Commission. If the
consent is denied by the State Commission, the PPA
shall become void as per Section 25(3) of the
Karnataka Reform Act and Section 86(b) of the 2003
Act. Accordingly, the second respondent had submitted
the PPA dated 3.5.2007 signed with the appellant before
the State Commission on 25.5.2007 for its consent.
(Emphasis supplied)
45. Again this Tribunal in Appeal No. 41 of 2018 - Hinduja National
Power Corporation Limited vs. Andhra Pradesh Electricity
Regulatory Commission and others decided on 7th January, 2020
held as under:-
“75. If the State Commission fails in discharging its duties
by deciding the matter without proper reasoning and
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 34 of 52

justification, it is nothing but failure of its duty. Since
proceedings before the State Commission are not in the
nature of a lis as in the case of a Civil Suit, it has to take
within its fold the interest of various stakeholders
concerned. Therefore, utmost duty of the State
Commission while discharging its functions must be
public interest and decide the matter on merits so far
as adoption of capital cost and Continuation
Agreement. The functions provided under Section
86(1)(b) of the Act is not merely a formality to approve
the Power Purchase Agreement. In other words, it does
not mean one of the parties to the petition can interdict the
implementation of Power Purchase Agreement at its
whims and fancies totally ignoring the fact that the
Commission's duty is to regulate electricity purchase
and procurement process of a distribution licensee
including the price at which electricity shall be
procured from generating companies through
agreements.
……………
80. As stated above, so far as the procurement of power
is concerned, it must be in the interest of the consumer.
Between April 2017 to January 2018 as against the
declared capacity, 3273.83 million units were delivered to
the Respondent DISCOMs from the Appellant's project.
Since it was conducive for AP DISCOMs to schedule and
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 35 of 52

take delivery of electricity for maintaining the retail supply
to its consumers the above number of units was taken by
the DISCOMs. To decide the matter pertaining to
capital cost or approval of Continuation Agreement,
one has to see whether it is in the interest of the
consumers at large. The State Commission is the
ultimate authority to decide procurement of power
including the price, but unfortunately the
Commission declined to decide the matter on merits.
In this process what Commission ought to have done in
OP No. 21 of 2015 is to determine whether the capital cost
and resultant tariff would be conducive to the interest of
the consumers at large, since it is incumbent to do so as
a regulatory authority. Therefore it was possible to first
decide O.P. No. 21 of 2015 on merits, and based on its
decision it should have proceeded to consider
Continuation Agreement instead of passing the impugned
order
…………………..
99. The Respondents contend that approval of Continuation
Agreement so that PPA of 1998 could get revived is based on
the principle enunciated in contingent contracts. According to
Respondents, the right if any to Appellant gets created only on
approval of Continuation Agreement dated 28.04.2016. They
contend that happening of approval is happening of some
future event, therefore question of neither of parties making
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 36 of 52

any offer and acceptance would arise. In a contingent contract
happening of something marks the moment at which a right is
created, so that the contract becomes enforceable. As against
this, Appellant contends that no doubt status of agreement
dated 28.04.2016 can be treated as a contingent contract. The
contract comes in to effect once approval is given by the
Commission. It is also not the case of Appellant that approval
of the state Commission is unnecessary. It is seen that
agreement for the purchase of energy was duly finalised and
agreed between the parties, which came in the form of a
document pertaining to confirmation of terms agreed. By virtue
of this agreement parties agreed to continue the amended and
restated PPA dated 15.04.1998 with modifications which are
clearly mentioned in the agreement. Parties also had
consensus that tariff will be as determined by the State
Commission in Petition No. 21 of 2015 filed by the Appellant.
The Continuation Agreement in a way becomes
concluded terms and conditions subject to approval by
the State Commission. It was not an inchoate or incomplete
contract as contended by AP DISCOMs."
(Emphasis supplied)
46. In Eswari Green Energy LLP Vs. Karnataka Electricity
Regulatory Commission and Ors., Appeal No. 180 of 2018 and
batch decided on 13th November, 2020, it was held by this Tribunal
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 37 of 52

"42.We do not agree with the broad argument of the
appellants that there is no need for separate approval of
the State Commission in respect of initiated PPAs simply
because the general format of the PPA had been approved
by the Commission on 22.7.2015. It cannot be overlooked
that the Commission regulates the purchase and procurement
process of each distribution licensee by virtue of the power
conferred on it under Section 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act,
2003. The statute saves the operation of the Karnataka
Electricity Reforms Act, 1999 by virtue of Section 185(3). The
provision contained in Section 17(1) of the Karnataka
Electricity Reforms Act, 1999 reads as under:
…………
44. A perusal of the statutory provisions and Rules
formulated thereunder shows that the distribution licensee can
procure power only in the manner approved and it is required
to place a proposed Power Purchase Agreement for approval
of the State Commission. The Regulation also prescribes a
timeframe for approval of the PPA. It also requires final version
of the PPA to be provided to the State Commission
……………..
47. In above context, reference may be made to following
observations of the Supreme Court in Tata Power Company
Limited vs Reliance Energy reported in (2009) 16 SCC 659,
while construing the functions of the Regulatory Commission
under Electricity Act, 2003:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 38 of 52

……………..
48. The documents produced show that all concerned
have throughout been of unanimous view that the power
purchase agreements which had been initiated required
the approval of the State Commission. Having sought such
approval though HESCOM, it is not permissible for the
appellants to now contend that no approval was required.
There is no doubt that approval of the State Commission
in respect of individual PPA is a condition precedent
without which the PPA cannot come into existence
though, the respondent HESCOM concedes, with post-facto
approval the PPA becomes operational retrospectively from
the date of the PPA.
49. The respondents are also right in submission that there is
no vested right to get approval of the PPA from the
Commission which is duty-bound to consider it in light of
statutory provisions and within regulatory framework.”
(Emphasis supplied)
47. Having regard to the clear legal position indicated by the
above noted legal provisions as well as law laid down by this
Tribunal as well as by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the above noted
judgement, it cannot be gain said that a PPA become effective only
upon getting approval from the State Commission and till then the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 39 of 52

parties are incapacitated from enforcing any rights or obligations
under the same.
48. Therefore, in this case, since the PPA was approved by the
Commission on 11th May, 2015, that day became the effective date
as per Article 10 of the PPA and, therefore, the scheduled date of
commissioning for the Appellant's power project was 10th March,
2016. The PPA was only a piece of paper till 11th May, 2015 i.e. the
date when it got approval from the Commission and, therefore,
neither the Appellant nor the 2nd Respondent could have initiated
any action on the basis of the PPA prior to the said date. The
Appellant was not expected to take any step for the execution of the
power project prior to the approval of the PPA by the Commission.
Had the Appellant initiated such step and incurred expenditure on
the same but later on the PPA was not approved by the Commission,
the time, efforts and money spent by the Appellant would have gone
into the drain. Therefore, the findings of the Commission in the
impugned order that the preliminary/preparatory works for execution
of the power project were not hampered for want of approval of the
PPA by the Commission, are absolutely unwarranted and perverse.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 200 of 2018 Page 40 of 52
